title: Wrong separator when multiple TCP clients simultaneously access to rigctld
body:
_Originally reported at https://sourceforge.net/p/hamlib/mailman/message/59187189/_

Hi,

I have several programs that interrogate rigctld simultaneously which
among other things request various radio parameters from my IC-7300
every second. With just one rigctld client program running I have no
issue, but I have discovered a number of issues that the developers may
or may not consider worth of rectification, when multiple rigctld
clients request radio parameters more of less simultaneously.

I can work around these issues, but nevertheless, I think they are worth
of reporting.

Hamlib version is  -  hamlib-w64-4.6.2

Windows (10) DOS Command to start rigctld is as follows: “rigctld -m
3073 -r COM4 -s 115200 -vvv”

These issues are probably all related or indeed have the same cause, but
I’ll list separately.

1 – Two Python programs are requesting the ptt status of the radio every
second. There is no synchronization between the two programs, so whether
or not they request the ptt status at the same time is hard to say. The
programs also request the frequency and mode of the radio.

Both programs request the ptt status using the “extended” method, ie the
TCP message is (in Python code). I’m using the optional ‘|’ separator as
can be seen from the code snippet

     sentBytes = rigctldSock.sendall(b'|t\n')
     response = rigctldSock.recv(1024)

The response should be                         b'get_ptt:|PTT: 0|RPRT 0\n'
however, every now and again, the response is of the form
b'get_ptt:\nPTT: 0\nRPRT 0\n'

which causes my parsing to fail. The response looks like the result as
if the ‘+’ separator was used, however this is not the case. Perhaps I
can avoid this by using the ‘+’ separator, but it shouldn’t be necessary.

2- Running the commercial LOG4OM program which is configured to use the
“Hamlib NET rigctl Stable” rig model, and one of my Python programs has
a similar effect as described in issue 1 above. I don’t of course know
the exact command that LOG4OM is using other than it is communicating to
rigctld on port 4532.

Also, the issue arises with multiple parameters. Once again, my program
uses the ‘|’ separator character. I don’t know what LOG4OM uses, or
indeed if it uses the “extended” or “default” method.

As before, expected responses are of the form ( for get_ptt and get_mode
commands)

     b'get_ptt:|PTT: 0|RPRT 0\n'
     b'get_mode:|Mode: LSB|Passband: 2400|RPRT 0\n'

however, occasionally the responses are

     b'get_ptt:\nPTT: 0\nRPRT 0\n'
     b'get_mode:\nMode: LSB\nPassband: 2400\nRPRT 0\n'

which fails my parsing due to the LF char unexpectedly replacing the ‘|’
char.

The cause is no doubt the same as in issue one. It may or may not matter
if two programs accessing rigctld use the same separator character.

3 – A similar issue arises if one rigctld TCP client is using the
“default” protocol and other the “extended” protocol more of less
simultaneously.

For example, I have one Python program accessing rig frequency using the
“extended” protocol which results in a response of this form

     b'get_freq:|Frequency: 1424840|RPRT 0\n'

at the same approximate time, the second client program uses the
“default” protocol which results in a response of this form

     b'1424840\n'

however, every once in a while, the response to the “default” protocol
results in this response

     b'1424840|\n'

It appears that the “default” response has been “infected” by the
separation character of the “extended” response due to the other client.

Of course, maybe I shouldn’t allow mixing of the two types of request,
but of course I have no easy way of knowing what any other arbitrary
program might be using that may simultaneously request radio parameters.

In summary, I feel these issues which probably all have the same root
cause may warrant looking at, but I will totally understand if it is
regarded as low priority or not worth fixing. In my case, I’ll probably
alter my programs to use the ‘+’ separator character that results in
‘\n’ characters separating the fields as I suspect this is what is
usually used.

Thanks for reading.
Rgds
Steve
VK3SPX

title: Legacy AGC Function mapping in Icom.c causes incorrect settings/readings on R75 (and others)
body:
What currently exists is a mapping of standard enumerated AGC_ values (e.g., SLOW, FAST, SUPERFAST, etc.) to alternate 'working' values. The comment in the defines seem to make it valid for the IC746 Pro and was added by Stephane a looong time ago. The problem is that applications using the standard mapping get undesirable results (such as selecting FAST and having the AGC turn OFF).

So there's a couple of possibilities:

1. This was solving a problem that was fixed using a combination of rig-specific configuration backends a long time ago: Standardizing the superset of settings from and dealing with the command codes on a radio-by-radio basis... and this was just forgotten about over time. or
 
2. This is still a valid thing for some older Icom transceivers (that I wouldn't know about). However, this is less likely, because there are so many other unassuming ways to do this. That said, this would take a tremendous amount of research amongst the complete field of Icom rigs in the library.

I'd like to recommend:
 
1. Restoring the original mapping to a one-to-one mapping (e.g., FAST to FAST, etc.) as well as including the rest of the enumerated values (they only mapped 4 of them) in icom.c and icom-defs.h - This should fix the immediate problem for many of the Icom radios.

2. Looking at the other rigs in the library, doing a quick grep to see which ones this would immediately affect. If the mapping was valid for some of these, generate rig-specific wrappers that intercept the AGC get/set routines and does this alternative mapping, and then call the standard icom.c routine for the other functions.

title: Cannot set frequency on FT857D using Python bindings
body:
Hello All,

As part of an effort to look at a local source of RFI, I'm trying to write a script that sweeps my transceiver (FT857D) across a range of frequencies, recording the signal strength at each frequency step.  Having written programmes with `hamlib` in the past in C, I thought I'd give the Python bindings a go.

Interestingly, although the script appears to connect to my rig, I cannot get consistent results when continuously polling the transceiver to update the frequency and read the S meter.  The guts of my approach are as follows
```python
def get_sig_strength(rig, frequency):
    logging.info(f"Setting frequency {frequency}")
    if rig.set_freq(RIG_VFO, int(frequency)) != Hamlib.RIG_OK:
        logging.warning("Cannot set frequency")
    sig_level = rig.get_level_i(Hamlib.RIG_LEVEL_STRENGTH)
    return sig_level

def freqsweep(rig, low, high, step):
    """Perform a frequency sweep on `rig`
       between `low`Hz and `high`Hz in steps
       of `step`Hz.
       :returns: a `numpy` matrix of signal strength versus frequency
    """
    freqs = np.arange(start=low, stop=high, step=step)
    return [[f, get_sig_strength(rig, f)] for f in freqs]
```
with the full code [here](https://gitlab.com/-/snippets/2377116).

It feels like Hamlib is not waiting long enough between successive commands for the rig to respond, but other than instrumenting my code with a bunch of `sleep()` statements (which work unreliably for reading `RIG_LEVEL_STRENGTH`, not for setting the frequency) I'm short for ideas.

A general question: many of the Python bindings don't work as expected given the Hamlib C++ doc, particularly wrt return codes -- above is a guess at error checking.  Is there a separate doc for the Python bindings to set me on the right path? 

73,

Chris

OS: Linux Mint 20.3
Python 3.8
Hamlib 3.3 (`python3-libhamlib2/focal 3.3-10build1 amd64)
Serial cable: USB-A to Yaesu mini-DIN connector, fine at 38400 baud with `rigctl` etc)
Rig: FT857D (hamlib ID 122)

title: GQRX remote interface
body:
Looking through some older issues, I notice people are using GQRX in concert with Hamlib-compatible applications. However, unless I've missed something, there doesn't appear to be a backend that is specifically designed to use the GQRX command set over TCP. There appears to be something similar that addresses using Airspy on SDRSharp (and gpredict), but I assume that is for Windows only.

Would it be advantageous for me to build a backend that specifically talks to GQRX's API, similar to what I already do in Frequency Browser? This backend would essentially use GQRX as an SDR bridge to osmosdr/gnuradio for Hamlib across other platforms, opening the door to Airspy, HackRF, BladeRF, RFSpace, SoapySDR, Funcube, RTL-SDR, etc.; as well as network-based SDRs.

Thoughts? Or again, have I missed something?

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

body:
Yes, it is possible to read the firmware version.
It is a two step process:

Identify the firmware being an UHSDR fw and not the "real" thing. For this there is "FT817" CAT command 0x42, which returns 5 bytes => "UHSDR".
Then it is safe to access the configuration variables of the UHSDR firmware mapped to EEPROM address above 0x7FFF. It stores the version number in 3 configuration variables (Major, Minor, Release). Access is through FT817 EEPROM reads above 0x7FFF as 16bit values.

By adding rx_vfo clients can call for rig operations freq, mode,etc using RX/TX vfo calls and not have to worry about what VFOs are available or how split has been set up or even if split has been turned on.

So the following will work
rig_set_freq(rig, RIG_VFO_RX, freq);
rig_set_freq(rig,RIG_VFO_TX, freq);
In non-split mode the VFO_TX call will be redundant and will not result in a CAT command since the cache will show the frequency is already set.
So anywhere else the client can turn on split and the same calls will still work.

title: rigtcld TCP port opening delay

labels.name: Critical
labels.description: A problem for common operations with WSJT-X, GPredict, RigPi, etc.

type.name: Bug
type.description: An unexpected problem or behavior

body:
Tested with:
Fedora 35
IC7300, USB connected to rig   (rig can be powered on by CI-V command)
IC706, USB RS232/CI-V converter connected (rig can NOT be powered on by CI-V command)

When rigctld is started and rig has power from power supply, but is **NOT** powered on by power button
it takes approx 11 seconds before rigctld opens TCP port 4532 for clients to connect.

If rig has power set **ON** by button **before rigctld is started** TCP port 4532 opens immediately for clients to connect.

It looks like rigctld will first poll rig to see that it is there before opening TCP port.
It should open TCP port immediately on startup and after that start to look if rig can be connected.

Current behavior is not good in cases where client program starts rigctld as a thread and then tries to catch it via TCP:4532.
There is no response if user has not powered his rig before starting client program and may lead to error "Can not connect to rigctld localhost:4532"

I can not see any harm if TCP port is open for clients right away from startup even there is no rig found yet.
Commands received before rig can be found should just get buffered until they can be delivered, or in other case just ignored and flushed away until rig is found.

title: Handling of power status and missing serial port

type.name: Bug
type.description: An unexpected problem or behavior

body:
Regarding discussion in #1302, @mdblack98 wrote the following:

```
This test case fails....

Power off on rig -- rigctld starts up OK
rigctld -m 1035 -r com37 -vv -Z

...

serial_open: Unable to open com37 - No such file or directory
port_open: serial_open(com37) status=-6, err=No such file or directory
rig_open: rs->comm_state==0?=0
rig.c(1042):rig_open returning2(-6) IO error

But running this fails -- and it should succeed, return -RIG_EPOWER, and not the rigctld side should not repeat the PS command -- seems we only ever need the PS command to execute at most two times but preferably only once.
rigctl -m 2 -vvvvv -Z

...

0000    5c 67 65 74 5f 70 6f 77 65 72 73 74 61 74 0a        \get_powerstat.
read_string_generic called, rxmax=1024 direct=1, expected_len=1
port_wait_for_data_direct(736): timeout=10,0
port_wait_for_data_direct(745): timeout=10,0
read_string_generic(): read failed, direct=1 - No error
netrigctl_get_powerstat: PS command failed (ret=-6) so returning RIG_POWER_ON
 1:rig.c(6233):rig_get_powerstat returning(0)
 1:netrigctl.c(257):netrigctl_open entered
netrigctl_transaction: called len=9
rig_flush_force: called for network device
network_flush called
write_block():1115 failed -1 - No error
IO error
IO error


2023-05-26T11:22:28.321707-0600: netrigctl_open: vfo_mode=0
2023-05-26T11:22:28.321752-0600: netrigctl_transaction: called len=12
2023-05-26T11:22:28.321788-0600: rig_flush_force: called for network device
2023-05-26T11:22:28.321824-0600: network_flush called
2023-05-26T11:22:28.321892-0600: write_block():1112 failed -1 - No error
2023-05-26T11:22:28.321937-0600:  1:netrigctl.c(295):netrigctl_open returning(-6) IO error

...
```


After looking at this, I think it's actually working (at least mostly?) as expected:

1) Note that this test case is about a missing serial port and *not* about rig being powered off (but serial port still being present).

2) rigctld (the daemon) will automatically close any client connection when it cannot open a rig. It will try to open the rig 1+3 times and then give up and close the rigctl client connection.

3) rigctl (the client using netrigctl backend) simply detects closing of the connection, fails and exits.

4) If the --ignore-err (or -Y) option is given to rigctl (the client), it will stay accepting commands and after any command it will cause rigctld (the daemon) to try to reopen the rig. If that fails, it will again detect closing of the connection, getting an I/O error (-6) internally from rig_open(). However, the resulting error code from rigctl (the client) is Invalid parameter (-1), since any command, such as rig_get_freq(), will return EINVAL error code if the rig is not open.

@mdblack98 Any comments on which of these are not correct behavior? After all, I think that if the serial port doesn't exist, rigctl error codes should reflect that condition (maybe instead return -6 I/O error?) and NOT indicate that power is off.

P.S. Regarding the other bug with rigctl client in netrigctl not following auto_power_on (or auto_power_off) is a simple fix, since automatic power on/off is not global behavior in rig.c (not 100% sure if it could be -- some rigs may need special handling in rig_open before commands can be supplied). I will push out a PR regarding those fixes soon.

title: Update TS890S/TS990S IF/MD command to SF/OM

labels.name: Backend
labels.description: Issues related to one or more backends.

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

body:
Since the "IF" and "MD" commands do not support new modes (PSK mode and
DATA mode) and sub-frequencies in their parameters, the TS-890S and
TS-990S have "SF" and "OM" commands as their replacements.

The "IF" and "MD" commands are not listed in the TS-990S/TS-890S PC
CONTROL COMMAND reference Guide, however, in order to maintain
compatibility with the KENWOOD SKY COMMAND SYSTEM, the "IF" and "MD"
commands also work (albeit imperfectly) as hidden functions in the
TS-990S and TS-890S.

For the above reason, the "IF" and "OM" commands of the TS-990S and
TS-890S remain in the future, but the "SF" and "OM" commands are
recommended.

Leo Fahmie KJ6HI DM03

JVCKENWOOD USA Corporation
Long Beach, CA 90810

title: TS-890S/990S change IF/MD command needed

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

body:
From Kenwood...

The "IF" and "MD" commands are implemented in both the TS-890S and TS-990S.

This is for compatibility reasons, such as the Sky command operations.

However, the parameters of these commands do not support new modes (such as PSK or DATA), or cross-mode split operation.

Therefore, the "PC CONTROL COMMAND Reference Guide" booklets of the TS-890S and TS-990S do not disclose "IF" or "MD", and recommend "SF" instead of "IF" and "OM" instead of "MD".

title: ICOM Clock set

labels.description: Issues related to one or more backends.

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

body:
Add ability to automatically set the clock to local or UTC for Icom rigs (and any others that may have a clock)
Perhaps get UTC from rig to determine which method to use (if current) and save it to hamlib_settings.
Time should be temporarily set to current and then wait for top of minute for final answer.
hamlib_settings value
[General]
clock=[UTC/Local] (note will be case-insensitive match)

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

body:
### Discussed in https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/discussions/1681
Originally posted by **ManoDaSilva** March 12, 2025 Hi! I've been messing around with professional ICOM radios (VHF/UHF) over the past years, and ended up reverse engineering the control protocol called PC-CMDv2. Multiple models are supported, including (but not limited to): - IC-F3161/4161 - IC-F5062/6062 - IC-F3400/4400 The control protocol is mostly aimed at handling digital (NXDN) messages, but is also able to change channel selection, display text on the radio, and even frequencies! My findings are documented here: https://github.com/MSF-Telecom/Telemetrinterface/blob/main/PC-CMDv2.md As it isn't a publicly available protocol, but has been reversed-engineered in a "clean-room" approach, is it worth pursuing its implementation on HamLib? I'd love to mess with a remote base using those radios, as they're readily available where I am... All the best, Mano - ON6RF

title: Packages like `autoconf-archive` may cause `bootstrap` and `configure` issues

type.name: Bug
type.description: An unexpected problem or behavior

body:
In reference to commit e641162, the installation of a `autoconf-archive` package (Debian name or similar) may cause Autconf macro (`macros/m4`) files to be overwritten when `bootstrap` is run.  The reason is due to there being some rather old macro files in our archive and the default behavior of `aclocal` (an Autoconf utility) is to replace them with newer versions it finds on the system.

### Why do we have old macro files?

They serve our purpose and we've not seen a reason to update.  This attitude may need to be adjusted.

### What are the symptoms?

Quite a number of files will be shown to be updated during a `bootstrap` run (Debian Stable):

``` console
$ ../hamlib/bootstrap 
Running 'autoreconf -i' to process configure.ac
and generate the configure script.
aclocal: overwriting 'macros/ax_cflags_warn_all.m4' with '/usr/share/aclocal/ax_cflags_warn_all.m4'
aclocal: installing 'macros/ax_compiler_vendor.m4' from '/usr/share/aclocal/ax_compiler_vendor.m4'
aclocal: overwriting 'macros/ax_cxx_compile_stdcxx.m4' with '/usr/share/aclocal/ax_cxx_compile_stdcxx.m4'
aclocal: overwriting 'macros/ax_lib_readline.m4' with '/usr/share/aclocal/ax_lib_readline.m4'
aclocal: overwriting 'macros/ax_pkg_swig.m4' with '/usr/share/aclocal/ax_pkg_swig.m4'
aclocal: installing 'macros/ax_prepend_flag.m4' from '/usr/share/aclocal/ax_prepend_flag.m4'
aclocal: overwriting 'macros/ax_pthread.m4' with '/usr/share/aclocal/ax_pthread.m4'
aclocal: overwriting 'macros/ax_python_devel.m4' with '/usr/share/aclocal/ax_python_devel.m4'
aclocal: installing 'macros/ax_require_defined.m4' from '/usr/share/aclocal/ax_require_defined.m4'
aclocal: installing 'macros/libtool.m4' from '/usr/share/aclocal/libtool.m4'
aclocal: installing 'macros/ltoptions.m4' from '/usr/share/aclocal/ltoptions.m4'
aclocal: installing 'macros/ltsugar.m4' from '/usr/share/aclocal/ltsugar.m4'
aclocal: installing 'macros/ltversion.m4' from '/usr/share/aclocal/ltversion.m4'
aclocal: installing 'macros/lt~obsolete.m4' from '/usr/share/aclocal/lt~obsolete.m4'
aclocal: installing 'macros/pkg.m4' from '/usr/share/aclocal/pkg.m4'
libtoolize: putting auxiliary files in AC_CONFIG_AUX_DIR, 'build-aux'.
libtoolize: copying file 'build-aux/ltmain.sh'
configure.ac:118: installing 'build-aux/ar-lib'
configure.ac:28: installing 'build-aux/compile'
configure.ac:149: installing 'build-aux/config.guess'
configure.ac:149: installing 'build-aux/config.sub'
configure.ac:37: installing 'build-aux/install-sh'
configure.ac:37: installing 'build-aux/missing'
amplifiers/elecraft/Makefile.am: installing 'build-aux/depcomp'
bindings/Makefile.am:108: installing 'build-aux/py-compile'
parallel-tests: installing 'build-aux/test-driver'
```

Git also shows the updates:

``` console
$ git status
On branch Hamlib-4.6.3
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
	modified:   macros/ax_cflags_warn_all.m4
	modified:   macros/ax_cxx_compile_stdcxx.m4
	modified:   macros/ax_lib_readline.m4
	modified:   macros/ax_pkg_swig.m4
	modified:   macros/ax_pthread.m4
	modified:   macros/ax_python_devel.m4

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	macros/ax_compiler_vendor.m4
	macros/ax_prepend_flag.m4
	macros/ax_require_defined.m4

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
```

Compare this to a *normal* run of `bootstrap` without an `autoconf-archive` package installed (Debian Stable):

``` console
$ ../hamlib/bootstrap 
Running 'autoreconf -i' to process configure.ac
and generate the configure script.
aclocal: installing 'macros/libtool.m4' from '/usr/share/aclocal/libtool.m4'
aclocal: installing 'macros/ltoptions.m4' from '/usr/share/aclocal/ltoptions.m4'
aclocal: installing 'macros/ltsugar.m4' from '/usr/share/aclocal/ltsugar.m4'
aclocal: installing 'macros/ltversion.m4' from '/usr/share/aclocal/ltversion.m4'
aclocal: installing 'macros/lt~obsolete.m4' from '/usr/share/aclocal/lt~obsolete.m4'
aclocal: installing 'macros/pkg.m4' from '/usr/share/aclocal/pkg.m4'
libtoolize: putting auxiliary files in AC_CONFIG_AUX_DIR, 'build-aux'.
libtoolize: copying file 'build-aux/ltmain.sh'
configure.ac:118: installing 'build-aux/ar-lib'
configure.ac:28: installing 'build-aux/compile'
configure.ac:149: installing 'build-aux/config.guess'
configure.ac:149: installing 'build-aux/config.sub'
configure.ac:37: installing 'build-aux/install-sh'
configure.ac:37: installing 'build-aux/missing'
amplifiers/elecraft/Makefile.am: installing 'build-aux/depcomp'
bindings/Makefile.am:108: installing 'build-aux/py-compile'
parallel-tests: installing 'build-aux/test-driver'
```

And `git status` is empty.

### Other gotchas

If the local repository gets the macros updated by `aclocal` that a command such as `git clean -dxf` will NOT revert the updates.  A command such as:

``` console
git restore macros/ax_cflags_warn_all.m4 macros/ax_cxx_compile_stdcxx.m4 macros/ax_lib_readline.m4 macros/ax_pkg_swig.m4 macros/ax_pthread.m4 macros/ax_python_devel.m4
```

will be necessary.

### Possible resolution?

Update the macro files carried in the repository, however, this may introduce other issues as behavior changes and additional macro dependencies occur.

Advise those running `bootstrap` (necessary only from a Git clone or purging the working tree of all generated files) to avoid having an `autoconf-archive` package installed (current "solution") or newer macro files available to `aclocal` on the system that are carried in this repository.

In `configure.ac` there is a macro call added in commit dd376a1267 that makes a C++11 compiler a mandatory build dependency:
> AX_CXX_COMPILE_STDCXX([11],[noext],[mandatory])

However the main library and the utilities are written in C and in fact after commenting out that line, they can be built.

It is currently undocumented what parts of Hamlib need a C++ or C++11 compiler:
* C++ bindings (can be disabled at configure time `--without-cxx-binding`, fix proposed in PR 1729)
* USRP (can be disabled at configure time `--enable-usrp`)
* INDI (can be disabled at configure time `--without-indi`)
 
There is something else that hasn't an explicit option in configure?

title: Different debug messages when entering functions

labels.name: Backend
labels.description: Issues related to one or more backends.

type.name: Task
type.description: A specific piece of work

body:
Some functions aren't using the macro `ENTERFUNC2` and are printing their own messages with different word or debug levels. I could prepare a pull request but since it involves 120 files changed, 959 insertions(+), 959 deletions(-) I think that it will be easier for @N0NB if he does the replacements himself with the commands below, so he can be sure that there aren't unrelated changes.

These differences make a little harder to scan the debug output.

At this moment:
* 869 lines have the verb "called" instead of "entered" as in `ENTERFUNC2`
  > rig_debug\(RIG_DEBUG_VERBOSE, "%s called\\n", __func__\);
* 89 lines have level `TRACE` instead of `VERBOSE` as in `ENTERFUNC2`:
   > rig_debug\(RIG_DEBUG_TRACE, "%s called\\n", __func__\);

```
VERBOSE='rig_debug\(RIG_DEBUG_VERBOSE, "%s called\\n", __func__\);'
TRACE_CALLED='rig_debug\(RIG_DEBUG_TRACE, "%s called\\n", __func__\);'
TRACE_ENTERED='rig_debug\(RIG_DEBUG_TRACE, "%s: entered\\n", __func__\);'
ENTERFUNC2='ENTERFUNC2;'
ENTERFUNC2_BODY='rig_debug\(RIG_DEBUG_VERBOSE, "%s\(%d\):%s entered\\n", __FILENAME__, __LINE__, __func__\);'

for VAR in VERBOSE TRACE_CALLED TRACE_ENTERED ENTERFUNC2 ENTERFUNC2_BODY; do echo "$VAR: $(grep -Er "${!VAR}" 2>/dev/null | wc -l)"; done

VERBOSE: 869
TRACE_CALLED: 89
TRACE_ENTERED: 3
ENTERFUNC2: 103
ENTERFUNC2_BODY: 1
```

My proposal is to use those environment variables above, `grep` and `perl` to replace some strings, and since `ENTERFUNC2` is defined in `misc.c`, to avoid editing files manually, use that macro only in the sources that already include it, and use the body of the macro  in the other cases, unless somebody knows an easy way to add `#include "misc.h"` (this can also be done later).
```
for VAR in VERBOSE TRACE_CALLED TRACE_ENTERED; do perl -pe "s/${!VAR}/$ENTERFUNC2/" -i $(grep -rl misc\.h); done

for VAR in VERBOSE TRACE_CALLED TRACE_ENTERED; do perl -pe "s/${!VAR}/$ENTERFUNC2_BODY/" -i $(grep -Erl "${!VAR}" 2>/dev/null); done
```

With the `perl` commands above, Hamlib builds, and the code has the following stats:
```
for VAR in VERBOSE TRACE_CALLED TRACE_ENTERED ENTERFUNC2 ENTERFUNC2_BODY; do echo "$VAR: $(grep -Er "${!VAR}" 2>/dev/null | wc -l)"; done

VERBOSE: 0
TRACE_CALLED: 0
TRACE_ENTERED: 0
ENTERFUNC2: 758
ENTERFUNC2_BODY: 307

grep -Er "rig_debug\(RIG_DEBUG_[^,]+" -oh | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
   2230 rig_debug(RIG_DEBUG_TRACE
   2212 rig_debug(RIG_DEBUG_ERR
   1851 rig_debug(RIG_DEBUG_VERBOSE
    191 rig_debug(RIG_DEBUG_WARN
     22 rig_debug(RIG_DEBUG_CACHE
     10 rig_debug(RIG_DEBUG_BUG
```

title: Split GitHub workflow script into multiple scripts

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

body:
Currently `.github/workflows/c-cpp.yml` run Continuous Integration (CI) on Ubuntu "latest" and MacOS "latest".  While this works and most configuration settings are shared, there are exceptions, particularly for MacOS which makes its stanzas a bit less straightforward than they could be.

I floated the idea to @dforsi and @markjfine in PR #1862 and both thought there is some merit to the idea.  [Daniele commented as follows](https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/pull/1862#issuecomment-3222094525):

> I think that's a good idea because we can see if a failure is only in one OS. It will also make it easier to add another workflow for Windows or Raspberry or something else. In the current workflow I like the sharing of the `--with` and `--enable` options, while overriding values for some steps, I don't know how to share them between different scripts. 

> I see that workflows can be executed manually with the trigger `on workflow_dispatch`, this can be useful to test the split scripts before having them run automatically, there isn't much documentation because it seems to work similar to `on push`/`on pull_request`: 

> https://github.blog/changelog/2020-07-06-github-actions-manual-triggers-with-workflow_dispatch/
> https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax?s=09#onworkflow_dispatch

With this approach I presume that each build will be self-contained with some apparent duplication between scripts.  This really isn't an issue as these files just sit in the repository and are not a part of the source distribution.

title: Configure script fails to detect libusb-1.0 on FreeBSD - hardcoded library name issue

type.name: Bug
type.description: An unexpected problem or behavior

body:
**Describe the bug**

- FreeBSD provides libusb-1.0 API through `-lusb` library name, not `-lusb-1.0`
- Configure script at line ~23326 hardcodes test for `-lusb-1.0` which fails on FreeBSD
- `pkg-config` correctly reports the library as `-lusb` but configure ignores this
- One workaround requires creating symlinks to existing libusb libraries: `ln -sf /usr/lib/libusb.so /usr/lib/libusb-1.0.so`, etc.

**To Reproduce**
1. `./bootstrap`
2. Run configure and examine the configure log for libusb issues:
```
$ ./configure --prefix=$HOME/local --with-python-binding --enable-pytest > /dev/null 2>&1
$ grep -A 20 -B 5 "libusb_init.*lusb-1.0" config.log
configure:23279: cc -c -g -O2   conftest.c >&5
configure:23279: $? = 0
configure:23281: result: yes
configure:23292: checking whether to build USB dependent backends
configure:23306: result: yes
configure:23326: checking for libusb_init in -lusb-1.0
configure:23355: cc -o conftest -g -O2    conftest.c -lusb-1.0   >&5
ld: error: unable to find library -lusb-1.0
cc: error: linker command failed with exit code 1 (use -v to see invocation)
configure:23355: $? = 1
configure: failed program was:
| /* confdefs.h */
| #define PACKAGE_NAME "Hamlib"
| #define PACKAGE_TARNAME "hamlib"
| #define PACKAGE_VERSION "4.7~git"
| #define PACKAGE_STRING "Hamlib 4.7~git"
| #define PACKAGE_BUGREPORT "hamlib-developer@lists.sourceforge.net"
| #define PACKAGE_URL "http://www.hamlib.org"
| #define HAVE_STDIO_H 1
| #define HAVE_STDLIB_H 1
| #define HAVE_STRING_H 1
| #define HAVE_INTTYPES_H 1
| #define HAVE_STDINT_H 1
| #define HAVE_STRINGS_H 1
| #define HAVE_SYS_STAT_H 1
| #define HAVE_SYS_TYPES_H 1
```

**Expected behavior**
configure runs to successful completion and Hamlib is ready to be compiled on the FreeBSD.

**Desktop (please complete the following information):**
 - OS: FreeBSD 14.3-RELEASE-p2
 - Client application: custom (via Python bindings)
 - Client application version: n/a

**Additional context**
Workaround:
```
LIBUSB_LIBS="-lusb" cf_with_cxx=yes ./configure \
    --prefix=$HOME/local \
    --with-python-binding \
    --with-libusb
```

How FreeBSD ports deals with this for version 4.5.5:
```
CONFIGURE_ARGS= --with-perl-binding \
                --with-tcl-binding --with-tcl=${TCL_LIBDIR} \
                --with-libusb \
                --with-python-binding
CONFIGURE_ENV=  LIBUSB_LIBS="-lusb" cf_with_cxx=yes
```

title: On FreeBSD, the configure script finds the libedit library but fails to detect the headers that come with it

type.name: Bug
type.description: An unexpected problem or behavior

body:
**Describe the bug**
Both editline and readline headers exist but configure didn't detect them, when it should default to using (editline).

**To Reproduce**
Steps to reproduce the behavior (please use `rigctl` with the `-vvvvv` option if at all possible and post the output under number 4 below):
1. `./bootstrap`
2. `./configure . . .`
3. `make`
4. Make output:
```
  CCLD     _Hamlib.la
Making all in tests
  CC       rigctl-rigctl.o
rigctl.c:668:9: error: use of undeclared identifier 'rl_readline_name'
  668 |         rl_readline_name = "rigctl";
      |         ^
```

**Expected behavior**
Make build runs to completion successfully.


**Desktop (please complete the following information):**
 - OS: FreeBSD 14.3-RELEASE-p2
 - Client application: custom (Python bindings)
 - Client application version: n/a

**Additional context**
The issue appears to be that configure's readline detection is incomplete - it finds the library but doesn't test for the headers. Since FreeBSD installs editline with readline-compatible headers in `/usr/local/include/readline/`, enabling `HAVE_READLINE_READLINE_H` should work.

Workaround:
```
# Force the configure result to recognize the editline readline.h
sed -i 's|/\* #undef HAVE_READLINE_READLINE_H \*/|#define HAVE_READLINE_READLINE_H 1|' include/hamlib/config.h

# Verify the change
grep "HAVE_READLINE_READLINE_H" include/hamlib/config.h
```

title: ICOM IC-7000 Stuck on Tx - Model Dummy?

**Describe the bug**
Starting rigctld with ic7000/digirig immediately goes to TX. rigctl cmds to change PTT state "T 0" fails. "t" cmd reports unsupported error. Rigctl "?" command shows proper model, with various supported and unsupported commands. DumpCaps reports "Model: Dummy".

I guess I'm not sure what the problem is... Stuck on TX, Model/DCD is mixed up, something else.

-vvvvv output from startup looks clean and as expected.. as far as I can tell.

If I start up WSJT-X TX issue goes away.. also basic functions (Band Change) work. Tx freaks out (seperate issue filed for this.).

Requesting guidance on how to collect further info or test scenaios.

title: SkyWatcher AZ-GTi (MC029) does not echo commands – SkyWatcher backend blocks waiting for echo
body:
### Description

When using Hamlib with SkyWatcher AZ-GTi mounts equipped with the MC029 motor controller, communication fails due to an incorrect assumption in the SkyWatcher rotator backend that the mount echoes commands.
This issue prevents rotctl / rotctld from working correctly with newer SkyWatcher Alt-Az mounts.

### Environment

-  Mount: SkyWatcher AZ-GTi
-  Motor Controller: MC029
-  Firmware: v3.54
-  OS: Windows 11
-  Hamlib version: 5.0.0~git (master)
-  Connection: USB (EQDir cable)
-  Baud rate: 9600
-  Flow control: None

### Problem Summary

The current SkyWatcher backend (rotators/skywatcher/skywatcher.c) assumes that all SkyWatcher mounts echo commands, and therefore performs two consecutive reads for every command:

-   Read echoed command
-   Read actual response

However, the MC029 motor controller does NOT echo commands.
As a result, the first read blocks until timeout, causing all commands to fail.

### Evidence

Using serial monitoring tools (AccessPort) and with direct confirmation from SkyWatcher SynScan App Team, it was verified that:

-   MC029 responds with only one response, starting with "=" or "!"
-   No command echo is sent
-   SynScan Pro works correctly because it does not expect an echo

### Temporary Workaround (Confirmed Working)

As a test, I modified skywatcher_cmd() to skip the echo read and read only the actual response.
Specifically, this block was removed/commented out:

>    // echo from the device
>    read_string(port, response, response_len, "\r", 1, 0, 1);

After this change:

-   rotctl p returns correct azimuth/elevation
-   rotctl P <az> <el> moves the mount correctly
-   No timeout, retry, or delay tuning is required

This confirms that the echo assumption is the root cause.

### Recommended Proper Fix (from SkyWatcher)

SkyWatcher confirmed that both echoing and non-echoing mounts exist, and provided two recommended approaches for compatibility.

**Option A (Preferred, robust parsing)**
This is the method currently used by SynScan Pro.

1. Send the command
2. Read incoming data byte-by-byte
3. Ignore all characters until "=" or "!" is received
4. Continue reading until "\r" (0x0D) is received
5. Characters between "=" (or "!") and "\r" form the valid response

This method:

- Works with legacy mounts that echo commands
- Works with MC029 and newer controllers that do not echo
- Does not require detecting echo behavior explicitly

**Option B (Echo-detection at initialization)**
 SkyWatcher also suggested an alternative approach:

1. During initialization, send a single test character (e.g. ":")
2. Check whether the mount echoes back that character
3. If echoed → enable echo-reading logic
4. If not echoed → skip echo reads

This approach also supports both legacy and newer mounts, but requires maintaining an additional per-device state flag.

### Why Timeouts / Delays Are Not the Cause

I tested modifications to:

- timeout
- write_delay
- post_write_delay
- retry logic

None resolved the issue unless the echo read was removed.
Therefore, this is a protocol parsing issue, not a timing issue.

### Request

Please update the SkyWatcher rotator backend to remove the unconditional echo read and adopt either:

- Option A: "=" / "!" anchored response parsing (preferred), or
- Option B: Echo-detection during initialization

I am happy to:

- Provide serial logs
- Provide my temporary patch
- Test any proposed fix on real MC029 hardware

Thank you for maintaining Hamlib.

### Additional Notes

SkyWatcher confirmed:

- Older Alt-Az mounts (Merlin, Virtuoso, Dob GOTO, etc.) may echo commands
- Newer controllers (MC029) do not echo commands
- Official SkyWatcher software already supports both cases correctly

title: rig_set_split_freq_mode does not set TX VFO frequency if frequency requested is the same that RX VFO already has.
body:
**Describe the bug**

Background: [JS8Call](https://github.com/JS8Call-improved/JS8Call-improved) in some configuration uses split mode to keep the audio frequency that gets sent to the rig in a sane range, "carrier" at 1500-2000 Hz.

Problem: When the user-selected audio carrier that is not in that range, all is fine. An appropriate split frequency is used. However, when the user later selects an audio carrier that already is in that range, so split operation would not be needed, the wrong old split frequency is re-used.

Here is what happens:

* JS8Call has set the RX or main VFO or VFOA to, say, 28078 kHz.
* From previous transmissions with an audio carrier in the, say, 1000-1500 Hz range, the TX or VFOB sits on 28077.5 kHz.
* Now a carrier in the 1500-2000 Hz range has been selected.
* JS8Call calls `rig_set_split_freq_mode` with the appropriate new frequency of 28078 kHz. As you may have noticed, this happens to be the frequency where the present VFOA sits.
* We believe that `rig_set_split_freq_mode` first reads the current frequency *of the wrong VFO* and decides no frequency change is needed, so ignores our request and leaves the split VFO at 28077.5 kHz.
* When we then push PTT, the wrong frequency 28077.5 is used instead of the correct 28078.

**To Reproduce**

Use hamlib calls to accomplish the following:

* Set the rig to receive mode.
* Configure split mode with VFOA for RX and VFOB for TX.
* Configure the main VFOA to some frequency.
* Set the auxiliary or split VFOB to some other frequency.
* Push PTT and check the rig that VFOB is used and the other frequency has been selected.
* Back to receive mode.
* While still in receive mode, set the auxiliary or split VFOB to the same frequency that is already VFOA's frequency, using `rig_set_split_freq_mode`.
* Push PTT and check which frequency is used.

**Expected behavior**

The rig shows the frequency that has been configured for VFOB.

Actually seen behavior: The rig shows the previous frequency of VFOB. VFOB frequency has not been changed.
(The calls to hamlib functionality have all reported success.)

We believe this code snipped causes our problem, as it reads the wrong VFO:

```
    // TX VFO may change after enabling split
    tx_vfo = rs->tx_vfo;

    rig_get_freq(rig, tx_vfo, &tfreq);

    if (tfreq == tx_freq)
    {
        rig_debug(RIG_DEBUG_TRACE, "%s: freq set not needed\n", __func__);
        ELAPSED2;
        RETURNFUNC2(RIG_OK);
    }
```

**Additional information**

Here is a combined debug log of JS8Call and hamlib showing the problem.

We believe the statement **rig_set_split_freq: freq set not needed** is wrong.

title: Yaesu FTX-1 split operation incompatibility with satellite tracking software (GPredict)

labels.name: Backend
labels.description: Issues related to one or more backends.

type.name: Task
type.description: A specific piece of work

body:
**Background**

FTX-1 has two independent VFOs labeled Main and Sub, but its internal split implementation behaves differently from conventional VFO-A/B radios.

Through repeated testing with GPredict + Hamlib (rigctl protocol), the following behavior has been consistently observed:

1. GPredict always issues the command S 1 1 to enable split operation when controlling uplink/downlink frequencies.
2. When Hamlib forwards this split command to the FTX-1 backend:
      -    The Sub VFO immediately enters TX/PTT state (red TX indicator turns on).
      -    While Sub is in this TX/PTT state, its frequency can no longer be changed.
3. As a result, it becomes impossible to control uplink and downlink frequencies independently on FTX-1 using split mode.
4. This behavior is specific to FTX-1 and does not match the expectations of satellite tracking software such as GPredict.

In other words:

- FTX-1 split mode forces the Sub VFO into active transmit state
- This prevents satellite software from continuously updating uplink frequency (Doppler correction)
- Therefore, FTX-1 cannot be used with satellite tracking software via standard split commands

**Proposed design direction**

To support FTX-1 correctly without breaking compatibility with existing applications:

- Hamlib should accept split commands from clients (e.g. S 1 1)
- But must not forward split mode commands to the FTX-1 radio
- Instead, Hamlib should:
    - Internally maintain a “logical split” state
    - Control Main and Sub VFO frequencies independently
    - Select the TX VFO logically (Main or Sub) without triggering hardware split/PTT on the radio

This approach would allow:

- GPredict and similar software to operate unchanged
- Correct uplink/downlink frequency control on FTX-1
- Avoidance of the Sub-VFO forced TX/PTT condition

**Summary**

FTX-1 requires model-specific handling in Hamlib because:

- Hardware split mode is incompatible with satellite Doppler control
- Standard split semantics used by satellite software cannot be applied directly
- A Hamlib-internal virtual split mechanism is necessary for correct operation

I am happy to assist with further testing, logs, or validation if this approach is considered acceptable.

title: GPIO PTT broken as of recent Linux kernel updates
body:
## Device

- Platform: Raspberry Pi 4B
- OS: Debian 1:6.6.20-1+rpt1 (2024-03-07) aarch64 GNU/Linux

## Background

The [sysfs GPIO interface](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/abi-obsolete.html#abi-sys-class-gpio) was removed in a recent Linux kernel update:

> This ABI is obsoleted by [testing/gpio-cdev](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/abi-testing.html#abi-file-testing-gpio-cdev) and will be removed after 2020.


See this blog post for more background info: https://waldorf.waveform.org.uk/2022/the-one-where-dave-breaks-stuff.html

I found out about this while trying to troubleshoot the below error and stumbling across this forum response: https://forums.raspberrypi.com/viewtopic.php?t=359540#p2157021

## Hamlib Error

The effect of this is that [the Hamlib code](https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/blob/master/src/gpio.c#L41) which relies on using `/sys/class/gpio` to manage GPIO ports will now throw an IO error.

```
$ sudo rigctl -P GPIO -p 4 -vv
GPIO4 direction (using /sys/class/gpio/gpio4/direction): No such file or directory
rig_open: cannot open PTT device "GPIO4"
rig_open: error = rigctl_parse.c(1974):set_conf return(0)
 1:rig.c(817):rig_open entered
rig_settings_get_path: path=/root/.hamlib_settings
rig_settings_load_all: settings_file (/root/.hamlib_settings): No such file or directory
rig_open: cwd=/home/aschuhardt
rig_open: /home/aschuhardt/hamlib_settings does not exist
rig_open: async_data_enable=0, async_data_supported=0
GPIO4 direction (using /sys/class/gpio/gpio4/direction): No such file or directory
rig_open: cannot open PTT device "GPIO4"
 1:rig.c(1237):rig_open returning(-6) IO error

IO error
 (null) No such file or directory
```

Attempting to manually open the GPIO device with the method used by Hamlib confirms that this is no longer possible:

```
$ sudo echo 4 > /sys/class/gpio/export      
echo: write error: Invalid argument
```

title: Hamlib test framework design

milestone.title: ARDC Hamlib improvement project: Milestone 1 - Test framework design
milestone.description:
Improve Hamlib Release Quality with an Automated Testing Framework

Issue: New Hamlib releases often inadvertently break previously functioning features due to
insufficient automated testing routines and difficulty of manually testing code changes in an
exhaustive way.

Solution: Develop an automated testing framework, allowing developers to define specific
command-response scenarios for any supported device (radio/rotator/amplifier), ensuring
changes do not regress existing functionality and that any new features added to Hamlib work
as expected.

Individual tests will be grouped into larger test suites where tests that are common to multiple
device models could be shared. Test suites would be written in YAML (structured text format) to make it easy to add tests without modifying the actual source code of Hamlib.

Test suites can be run either using emulated device responses or alternatively against real
hardware when such hardware is available. This will make it possible to verify that the
emulated tests actually reflect the hardware.

The deliverables of this milestone include: a design document regarding how the test framework functions, the key technical implementation choices (e.g. source code structure, language and dependencies) and example test suites in YAML format.

body:
This is the main issue for ARDC Hamlib improvement project [Milestone 1 - Test framework design](https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/milestone/24) - plans and discussion.

# Project background

* See ARDC grant: https://www.ardc.net/apply/grants/2025-grants/hamlib-stability-enhancements-and-sdr-transceiver-support/
* See Open Collective page: https://opencollective.com/hamlib-stability-enhancements-and-sdr-transceiver-support

The project backlog is available in: https://github.com/orgs/Hamlib/projects/1 (still in progress)

# Description

**Goal:** Improve Hamlib Release Quality with an Automated Testing Framework

**Issue:** New Hamlib releases often inadvertently break previously functioning features due to insufficient automated testing routines and difficulty of manually testing code changes in an exhaustive way.

**Solution:** Develop an automated testing framework, allowing developers to define specific command-response scenarios for any supported device (radio/rotator/amplifier), ensuring changes do not regress existing functionality and that any new features added to Hamlib work as expected.

Individual tests will be grouped into larger test suites where tests that are common to multiple device models can be shared. Test suites will be written in YAML (structured text format) to make it easy to add tests without modifying the actual source code of Hamlib.

Test suites can be run either using emulated device responses or alternatively against real hardware when such hardware is available. This will make it possible to verify that the emulated tests actually reflect the hardware.

The deliverables of this milestone include: a design document regarding how the test framework functions, the key technical implementation choices (e.g. source code structure, language and dependencies) and example test suites in YAML format.

#  Development Process

* GitHub issues in the main Hamlib repository will track the project's progress, milestones, and deliverables transparently.
* All code contributions will be made as GitHub Pull Requests against the main Hamlib repository for final community review and comments
* All code will be licensed under the existing GNU LGPL 2.1 (or later) license

# Design

Please look at the comments below for an early specification and YAML test specification examples!

title: Unit test tooling in Hamlib

labels.name: Question
labels.description: Issues on a fact finding mission

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

body:
As a part of the ARDC improvement project tasks (for example task #1940), I'd very much like to start writing unit tests to verify the new application logic and features work as expected. This kind of test code is tightly-coupled with the Hamlib C (or potentially C++ API bindings) code, so it's beneficial that it is written in the same language as the original code, as it will be calling the public API functions of Hamlib directly.

Currently, the only test code that Hamlib codebase contains, are the simulators (which are more in the category of integration or system testing) and some Python test code that primarily tests the Python bindings (again, more for integration/system testing I'd argue).

In order to help writing unit tests, I'd propose we use some simple unit testing framework that supports both C and C++ testing to get the following benefits:

1) clear structure for declaring and grouping tests
2) standardized test assertions
3) standardized way to run tests
4) test result reporting (success / failure with error messages)
5) integration with autotools (current build framework) -> automake uses TAP protocol
6) integration with CI (GitHub Actions) -> GHA uses JUnit reporting for test results

One possible choice is to go with a very simple, single-header library, such as Acutest: https://github.com/mity/acutest

Please see the GitHub README of Acutest for examples on assertions and how tests are declared - it uses simple C macros for most things (just like many other C/C++ unit test frameworks I've seen), but is otherwise very "unintrusive" as it's just a single header file we can include in the sources. Additionally, it includes simple support for both TAP and JUnit reporting. Both C and C++ are supported.

Other suggestions are welcome!

title: Reduce development overhead by supporting only extended responses in Hamlib daemons in newly introduced commands

labels.name: Question
labels.description: Issues on a fact finding mission

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

body:
All Hamlib daemons (rigctld, rotctld and ampctld) support two types of responses for most commands (though even this is not 100% consistent, see below).

## Proposal

I propose we stop supporting the non-extended responses in **all new commands added to any Hamlib daemon**. The existing commands would still work as expected (current API won't be broken), but new commands would require use of `+` prefix to work.

The non-extended response format introduces considerable burden on maintenance and development (we'd have to support two different kinds of responses) with little to no gain: the non-extended responses are rather difficult to handle predictably by clients reading the TCP stream. See below for a more detailed analysis.

### New behavior

Hamlib daemons handle unknown commands in a rather "passive" way, by simply not returning any response (which itself is bad, but we can't really fix it right now without breaking the daemon command API), so with any new commands not supporting non-extended responses, the command would be silently ignored.

Examples:

No response to a new command that doesn't support non-extended responses:
```
\new_command
```

Extended response with a new command:
```
+\new_command
new_command:
Response: 1
RPRT 0
```

## Non-extended response format and its drawbacks

The non-extended response is usually (but not always!) a one-line response with no indication of field names or any metadata. The command may be a short form (single char) or long form command (starting with a backslash `\`), e.g.:

```
f
145000000
```

```
\get_freq
145000000
```

However, there are exceptions to the single-line approach, such as...

Multi-line responses:
```
\get_split_freq_mode
0

0
```

Caps dump returning extended response always: (Would likely be impossible to parse otherwise)
```
1
Caps dump for model: 1
Model name:	Dummy
Mfg name:	Hamlib
...
RPRT 0
```

As we can see, the challenge with this format is that it's not consistent and it's difficult to parse:

* Critical flaw: Client parser needs to know exactly what to expect in the response, since there is no indication of where the response ends -> With a TCP connection, there has to be some framing present to know where response ends.
* More complex responses, ones with several or tens of fields, become difficult to represent and to parse
* The response format is difficult to extend, as there is no indication of what values represent what information -> clients will be easily confused even if new fields are added in the response
* Even right now, responses are not consistent: single-line and multi-line responses are mixed + caps dump returning extended responses always.

## Extended responses

The extended response mode is enabled with a plus char `+`, leading to a more structured response format, including an indicator for the end of the response (`RPRT [CODE]`). Both of these features make usage of extended responses basically a must in TCP clients.

Here is a good example of how the extended response makes parsing the responses easy.

Non-extended response with no indication of where the response ends or the meaning of the values returned:
```
\get_vfo_info VFOA
145000000
FM
15000
0
0
```

Extended response with repeated command on the first line, response as key-value pairs and `RPRT 0` ending the response.
```
+\get_vfo_info VFOA
get_vfo_info: VFOA
Freq: 145000000
Mode: FM
Width: 15000
Split: 0
SatMode: 0
RPRT 0
```

title: dumpcaps.c and dumpstate.c have many similar lines

labels.name: Shared library
labels.description: Issues related to the shared library

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

body:
It appears that many lines code in `dumpcaps()` and `dumpstate()` differs only in the use of a pointer and/or different "astyle" settings.

Examples:
```diff
-    fprintf(fout, "Has Init:\t%c\n", rs->rig_init != NULL ? 'Y' : 'N');
+    fprintf(fout, "Has Init:\t%c\n", rig->caps->rig_init != NULL ? 'Y' : 'N');
...
-    for (i = 0; i < HAMLIB_TSLSTSIZ && !RIG_IS_TS_END(rs->tuning_steps[i]); i++)
+    for (i = 0; i < HAMLIB_TSLSTSIZ
+            && !RIG_IS_TS_END(rs->tuning_steps[i]); i++)
```

`dumpcaps.c` has more code than `dumpstate.c` but it's unclear what their purpose is, except implementing the command with the same name in `rigctl`.

To fix this issue, either:
* document why they must be different

or
* refactor common code

the frequency and modes are jumping from one to an other, e.g the frequency jumps from 7 MHz before start to 20 and then to 200MHz or 700 MHz within a few hundred milliseconds after start -- this happens all after start of rigctld without any further interaction! -- Momentary this backend is unusable!

2. The function that fails, i.e. `rig_open`, `rig_set_freq`, `rig_get_freq`, etc.: all functions

f

RPRT 0

f
20070200

rig is set to 7020,000 kHz and stable in this experiment 

**Expected behavior**
stable operation on the set frequency

title: Hamlib Python3 bindings unfit to retrieve rig capabilities.
body:
A Python3 application inside an amplifier in the past used to retrieve lists of manufacturers and rigs from Hamlib by scanning through all rigs and retrieving manufacturer and rig type.
This was used in a menu to pick a brand and a rig of that brand.
This worked with Hamlib installed as a Debian package in 'Trixie'.
After compiling Hamlib 4.7.0 with its Python3 bindings, this no longer works.
Hamlib.py is lacking the equivalent of the RIG_TYPE defines, and is lacking essential methods that link to e.g. get_cap and rig_load_all_backends. 
On first sight this seems to be caused by a very restrictive setting of SWIG, in ignore.swg, where virtually all is thrown out, to only put a few things back.
Have now rewritten my Python code to directly address libhamlib.so.4 using ctypes.CDLL("libhamlib.so.4"), avoiding use of the Hamlib Python bindings. But the idea of having Python3 bindings to Hamlib is of course to have complete access to the underlying functions and data in a Pythonic way.

title: Yaesu FTX-1 incorrect CAT controls for meters
body:
**Describe the bug**
While trying to create a Python application that uses hamlib 4.7 with an FTX-1 Field, I discovered that most of the meter readings did not work. For example ALC always returns 0 when the radio is displaying 9.

After looking into the code and the CAT manual, I discovered the meters are not implemented correctly. The RM command is on page 23 of the current CAT manual, and uses RM4 for ALC. The current backend tries to use RM2, which is the S-meter for the SUB side of the radio. 

The problem is the section of ftx1_audio.c starting at line 207.

**To Reproduce**

1. `rigctl` model: 1051

body:

title: FTX-1: get_mode returns 0 passband, set_mode ignores width — SH not wired into mode path
body:
## Problem

The FTX-1 driver delegates mode handling to `newcat_set_mode` / `newcat_get_mode`, which do not use the `SH` (bandwidth) CAT command. This means:

1. **`m` (get_mode)** always returns 0 for passband width, even though the radio has a specific filter width set via `SH`
2. **`M MODE WIDTH`** sets the mode via `MD` but silently ignores the width parameter — the radio's filter bandwidth is not changed

The FTX-1 firmware treats `MD` (mode) and `SH` (bandwidth) as completely independent commands. `MD` never touches bandwidth, and querying `MD` never returns it. The `SH` command works correctly for both set and read — it just isn't called.

## Workaround

Users can set bandwidth by sending `SH` directly via raw CAT (`w SH0019;` for code 19 = 3200 Hz in SSB mode), and read it back with `w SH0;`. But this bypasses the standard Hamlib mode/passband interface.

## SH Lookup Table (from CAT reference)

SH uses mode-dependent codes:

- **SSB/DATA**: codes 0–21 (200 Hz to 4000 Hz)
- **CW**: codes 0–17 (50 Hz to 3000 Hz)
- **RTTY**: codes 0–12 (50 Hz to 2400 Hz)
- **AM**: codes 0–3 (3000 Hz to 9000 Hz)
- **FM**: code 0 only (no selectable bandwidth)

## Expected Fix

- `newcat_get_mode` (or FTX-1 override): query `SH` alongside `MD`, map the SH code to Hz for the passband return
- `newcat_set_mode` (or FTX-1 override): when width != 0, find the nearest valid SH code for the target mode and send `SH` after `MD`

## Environment

- Radio: Yaesu FTX-1, firmware v1.08+
- Hamlib driver: `rigs/yaesu/ftx1/ftx1.c` (delegates to newcat framework)

title: FTX-1: ftx1_set_channel uses MW, which firmware rejects on all channels
body:
## Problem

`rig_set_channel` on an FTX-1 always fails because the driver's `ftx1_set_channel` implementation builds and sends the `MW` (Memory Write) CAT command, which the FTX-1 firmware rejects universally with `?;` — on every channel, in every mode, regardless of parameters. The channel never gets written.

## Empirical evidence

Tested directly against a live FTX-1 (field head + Optima/SPA-1, firmware MAIN v1.12) at 115200 bps. Sent the exact MW command string the driver would build:

```
tx:  MW00005014250000+0000002120000;
rx:  ?;
```

MR readback of the target channel afterward confirms nothing was written:

```
tx:  MR00005;
rx:  ?;
```

This behavior is reproducible across every channel number and every mode I tested. `MW` appears to be completely non-functional on current FTX-1 firmware.

## Current broken code

File: `rigs/yaesu/ftx1/ftx1_mem.c`

`ftx1_set_channel()` at line 147 builds a 30-char MW command with freq, clarifier, mode, tone, and shift parameters, then calls `newcat_set_cmd()` at line 246. The firmware rejects the command and the function returns `-RIG_EPROTO`. No channel state is modified.

Related: the `DC` (DCS code) command is similarly firmware-broken — all variants return `?;` — and must be replaced by `CN` with `P2=1`. The FTX-1 driver already handles DCS via `CN` correctly in `ftx1_ctcss.c`, so the memory-write rewrite will follow the same approach.

## Proposed fix — VFO-B + BM workaround

The FTX-1 supports memory write via an indirect sequence that empirically works:

1. `MC<ch>;` — point the "last-selected channel" cursor at the target slot. Ignore `?;` if the slot is currently unprogrammed; the cursor still updates.
2. `VM000;` — force VFO mode (MC may have entered memory mode).
3. Configure **VFO-B** to the target state:
   - `FB%09.0f;` for frequency
   - `MD1<mode_char>;` for mode
   - `CT1<mode>;` + `CN10<idx>;` for CTCSS (FM channels only)
   - `CT13;` + `CN11<code>;` for DCS
   - `OS1<shift>;` for repeater shift
4. `BM;` — copy VFO-B state to the last-selected memory channel.

VFO-B is used rather than VFO-A so the operator's primary RX VFO is untouched. A production version should snapshot VFO-B at entry and restore it on exit (including error paths).

## Validation of the workaround

Verified end-to-end on the same live radio:

```
# Starting state: channel 1 = 7.000.000 LSB (existing memory)
tx:  MC000001;                  rx:  ''        (select ch 1, enter memory mode)
tx:  VM000;                     rx:  ''        (back to VFO mode)
tx:  FB007050000;               rx:  ''        (VFO-B = 7.050 MHz)
tx:  MD11;                      rx:  ''        (VFO-B = LSB)
tx:  BM;                        rx:  ''        (commit)

# Verify
tx:  MC000001;                  rx:  ''
tx:  FA;                        rx:  FA007050000;   ← channel 1 now 7.050
tx:  MD0;                       rx:  MD01;          ← mode preserved

# Restore channel 1 to 7.000 (reverse with the same sequence)
# Final: MR reads 7.000 LSB again, VFO-B restored to original state
```

Channel 1 was successfully rewritten and restored — the workaround is proven on hardware.

## Known scope gap

The existing MW path also handles clarifier/RIT state for the channel. Whether `BM` propagates clarifier state to the memory slot hasn't been empirically verified yet. The planned rewrite handles freq + mode + CTCSS + DCS + shift; clarifier persistence for channels is a potential follow-up if users report it missing.

## Environment

- Radio: Yaesu FTX-1 field head + Optima/SPA-1, firmware MAIN v1.12
- Hamlib: current master (post-merge of #2031)

I have a working rewrite ready and will submit it as a follow-up PR.

title: Icom: Filter commands (0x1A 0x03) fail in CWR mode (missing RIG_MODE_CWR in bitmasks)
body:
Tested with: 4.7.0 

ICOM set filter fails in CWR mode

I had a look at the code after github copilot tried to identify the issue . I appologize in advance if the code below isn't the real reason.  
BTW I noticed IC 7760 is still in alpha state. If you need a tester, let me know. I have one.


**Description:**
On Icom rigs, sending filter width commands via `rigctl/rigctld` (e.g., `W 500`) works correctly when the rig is in **CW** mode, but is ignored when the rig is in **CWR** (CW Reverse) mode.

**Technical Analysis:**
The issue lies in `rigs/icom/icom.c`. Several functions that handle DSP filter width calculations specifically omit `RIG_MODE_CWR` from their mode bitmasks.

1.  In `icom_get_dsp_flt()` (around line 2084), the check for CW-like modes excludes `CWR`:
    ```c
    else if (mode & (RIG_MODE_CW | RIG_MODE_USB | RIG_MODE_LSB | ...))
    ```
2.  In `icom_set_dsp_flt()` (around line 2127), the same omission exists:
    ```c
    else if (mode & (RIG_MODE_CW | RIG_MODE_USB | RIG_MODE_LSB | ...))
    ```

Because `CWR` is not matched, the functions fall through to the `else` block, which logs "unknown mode" and returns `RIG_OK` without sending the CI-V command to the radio.

**Suggested Fix:**
Update the mode bitmasks in `icom_get_dsp_flt` and `icom_set_dsp_flt` to include `RIG_MODE_CWR` alongside `RIG_MODE_CW`.

**Note:**
I am unable to compile or test Hamlib from source at this time, so I am reporting this as an issue for a maintainer to implement and verify.

title: New JSON protocol for Hamlib

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

body:
(Copied over from discussion in #1853 - as the JSON protocol can be implemented mostly independently from dump_caps/dump_state changes)

In Hamlib 5.0, I'd suggest we'd start a transition to machine-parseable JSON protocol. The reason is that current Hamlib protocol is text-based (more in human-readable format), which makes it difficult to parse and for the (Hamlib client) parsers to stay compatible with new Hamlib changes.

Currently, implementing a client for rigctld/rotctld/ampctld daemons requires using of the extended response format, so that the end of the response can be reliably detected (e.g. `RPRT`) and the response values are in a rather arbitraty key/value-format. Additionally, parsing `\dump_caps` capabilities requires implementing a complex parser for all the different kinds of notations used. This is very sub-optimal and we could benefit from the widely-used JSON format to express all commands and responses (including capabilities) in a well-structured manner. JSON is already used in Hamlib in the "snapshot data" (rig state + spectrum data), so we can use the existing, embedded JSON library for this!

What's even better, clients could more dynamically adapt to new fields introduced in new Hamlib releases (especially in the device capabilities data) by just ignoring any fields they don't recognize. Any existing, named fields should of course keep their format compatible as long as protocol compatibility is necessary.

My proposal: (separate from the #1853 dump_caps/dump_state discussion)
 
Allow use of JSON in all commands and responses. We'd still keep the current response formats (short + extended), but add a new "JSON" format, which would be opt-in.

For example, now `+\get_freq` gives you the extended response like:
```
Frequency: 145000000
```

To use the JSON format, the command should simply be a JSON object, e.g. (we'd keep the command names intact, I think there's no need to change them)
```
{"cmd": "get_freq"}
```

Response:
```
{"freq":145000000, "result": 0}
```

For commands that take arguments, I propose to remove the "positional parameters" (= an array) and to use the full power of JSON with keys, e.g.

To use the JSON format, the command should simply be a JSN object, e.g.
```
{"cmd": "set_freq", "freq": 144800000}
```

Response would always contain at least the `result` field to indicate finished execution and its status: (response could optionally also echo back the given parameters)
```
{"freq":144800000,"result":0}
```

The parser could easily detect JSON commands by checking the first character of the command, e.g. `{` for JSON and `+` for extended response, `\` for long format commands or one of the single char commands.

This allows clients to migrate to JSON format command-by-command (e.g. only use JSON for dump_caps for a start), making gradual migration possible.

The command and response keys (in JSON objects) could use short, but still easy-to-read wording to minimize extra network traffic, e.g. `command` -> `cmd`, `frequency` -> `freq` and so on.

This will of course need some mappings between the existing command handling and JSON, but I think it's completely doable. It's likely we could extract the parsing logic of Hamlib commands to a more modular, reusable place for all of the device types/daemons.

NOTE: This protocol would still keep the **synchronous** way of communicating with Hamlib, so that only one command can executed at a time and each command will receive a response. For asynchronous responses, we should use the existing "snapshot data" and UDP packet containing JSON - additional message types can be implemented in the UDP/JSON protocol if needed.

I will add a proposal of the capabilities data JSON response here in a separate message.

EDIT: We could use a separator character (for example the null / byte 0x00) as end-of-command and end-of-response for the JSON format, just to make parsing easy for both Hamlib and the clients. This way the parser, after detecting a `{` as the first character of a command (or the same for a client detecting that in the response), could simply read the data stream until the separator character arrives. Otherwise parsing would require knowledge of the JSON object format, which is again quite sub-optimal.

title: The readline detection sets HAVE_LIBREADLINE=1 even when using libedit, but the code assumes full readline compatibility

labels.name: Utilities
labels.description: Issues regarding the included utilities in the `testing` directory.

type.name: Bug
type.description: An unexpected problem or behavior

body:
**Describe the bug**
Compile fails due to undeclared identifier `rl_readline_name`.

**To Reproduce**
1. `./bootstrap`
2. `./configure . . .`
3. `make`
4. Make output:
```
  CCLD     _Hamlib.la
Making all in tests
  CC       rigctl-rigctl.o
rigctl.c:668:9: error: use of undeclared identifier 'rl_readline_name'
  668 |         rl_readline_name = "rigctl";
      |         ^
```

**Expected behavior**
Make runs to successful completion.

**Screenshots**

**Desktop (please complete the following information):**
 - OS: FreeBSD 14.3-RELEASE-p2
 - Client application: custom (Python bindings)
 - Client application version: n/a

**Additional context**
The problem seems to be that none of the standard readline/editline headers are being included because configure didn't find `HAVE_READLINE_READLINE_H` or `HAVE_READLINE_H`. But the code in `rigctl.c` has this logic:
```
#ifdef HAVE_LIBREADLINE
#  if defined(HAVE_READLINE_READLINE_H)
#    include <readline/readline.h>
#  elif defined(HAVE_READLINE_H)
#    include <readline.h>
#  else
extern char *readline();
#  endif
#endif
```
Since neither header macro is defined, it only declares` readline()` but not `rl_readline_name`.

Workaround:

```
# Add the missing extern declaration
sed -i '/extern char \*readline();/a\
extern char *rl_readline_name;' rigctl.c

# Verify the change
grep -A 2 -B 2 "extern.*readline" rigctl.c
```

title: Incorrect output from netrigctl depending on the language environment
body:
I am using the wfview program on my Linux computer to connect to my ICOM transceiver.
Digi-mode programs such as FreeDV, FlDigi, and QSSTV connect to wfview’s rigctl server via Hamlib.NET (m=2). This works to some extent. The programs can also read the transceiver’s frequency. However, the digi-mode programs are unable to change the transceiver’s frequency.

**Error and Expected behavior**
An analysis of the data traffic has revealed that, for example, the command `F 7177000,000000` is issued to change the frequency. However, the correct command here would be `F 7177000.000000`.

The command is likely issued from the Hamlib module `netrigctl.c`. Line 968:
``` c
SNPRINTF(cmd, sizeof(cmd), “F%s %‘FREQFMT’\n”, vfostr, freq);
```
where `FREQFMT = “lf”`     from `hamlib/rig.h`

However, the floating-point number generated is adapted to the current locale.
Since my `LC_NUMERIC` is set to `de_DE.UTF-8`, the number is generated with a comma.

I found a workaround where I change the Linux environment variable to `LC_NUMERIC="C"` before starting a Digi-Mode program, but this may also have its disadvantages elsewhere.

Hamlib should ensure that all inputs and outputs in communicating data, involving floating-point numbers, always use a decimal point, regardless of the language environment. There is reason to fear that this error occurs not only here, but also in other places and modules.

**Software**
`rigctl Hamlib 4.7.1 2026-04-15T20:20:01Z SHA=d042479a9 64-bit`
[wfview v2.22rc1](https://github.com/eliggett/wfview/releases/tag/v2.22rc1)

title: Problematic `pthread_cancel` calls may result in dead-lock and memleak
body:
As part of the effort getting hamlib to run on Android, I came across several calls of `pthread_cancel` that can't be provided Android. As mentioned by a thread (https://groups.google.com/g/android-platform/c/Cq05PaLaZbE):

> In all cases, be sure to properly release resources when exiting thr
thread. 99% of the code that uses pthread_cancel I have seen leaks
memory, or even locks, in certain circumstances.

Upon digging more into the hamlib codebase, it seems the problem exists: one may never know where the thread will get cancelled, even in a mutex scope. E.g. the program could be cancelled during sleeping skipping mandatory cleanups. POC:  https://paste.armbian.com/itoviroyup.cpp

In https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/blob/b43eca4e48e85c7ec963e88553dc064241a4bffd/src/rig.c#L8871, the data handler tries to clean up the allocated mem after a sleep, as replicated by the above POC. However, it may also stop anywhere in the mutex scope https://github.com/Hamlib/Hamlib/blob/b43eca4e48e85c7ec963e88553dc064241a4bffd/src/rig.c#L8835 which may dead-lock the rig.

Fortunately there are already flags (`XXX_data_handler_thread_run`) we can take advantage of to gracefully end the thread in controllable ways, so I suggest we just refactor out any `pthread_cancel` calls.
